pages.title: GENERAL Definition

blocks.text: GENERAL Definition
The main function of respiration is to ensure gas exchanges: intake of O₂ and elimination of CO₂ = respiratory activity is rhythmic, automatic and permanent.
Ventilatory activity is generated by neural networks in the brainstem
The objective of ventilatory regulation is to maintain homeostasis by ensuring the stability of partial pressures in O2 (PaO₂), CO2 (PaCO₂) as well as blood pH, within narrow limits.
It thus makes it possible to constantly adapt the frequency and amplitude of respiratory movements to the needs of the body.

pages.title: GENERAL Respiratory control

blocks.text: GENERAL Respiratory control
Respiratory automation:
- Modular according to the needs of the organization
- Coordination with other functions: Swallowing, Phonation
factors modulating respiration:
- metabolic activity: sleep, physical exercise
- environmental changes: acclimatization and adaptation to extreme conditions
- pathological factors

pages.title: GENERALFeedback loop

blocks.text: GENERALFeedback loop
Receptors:-Mechanoreceptors = ventilatory mechanics-Chemoreceptors = blood gas composition
Afferent pathways: transmit information from receptors to respiratory centers
Respiratory centers: integrate and coordinate information
Efferent pathways: from respiratory centers to muscles
Effectors: respiratory muscles responsible for ventilatory work = adjust ventilation
Feedback: the new ventilation modifies the activity of the receptors = feedback loop

pages.title: RESPIRATORY CENTERS

blocks.text: RESPIRATORY CENTERS

pages.title: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers

blocks.text: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers
-Brain stem = the bulb and the protuberance (bridge).
- made up of neural networks responsible for ventilatory rhythmogenesis.
- their activity ensures rhythmic, automatic and permanent breathing.
- highlighted by the experiments of staged sections.
- their functioning can be modulated by peripheral and central inputs (chemoreceptors, cortex, etc.).

pages.title: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers

blocks.text: Bulbar respiratory centers = two dense, bilateral aggregations of respiratory neurons:
Dorsal Respiratory Group (DRG):
-located in the posterior part of the bulb, in the nucleus of the solitary tract
-integrates peripheral afferents (via IXth and Xth cranial pairs)
- sending efferences to the phrenic motor neurons and to the ventral respiratory group (GRV),
Made up mainly of inspiratory neurons.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers
Ventral respiratory group (GRV): located caudally to the GRD,
Upper part contains the pre-Bötzinger complex consisting of:
pacemaker cells, capable of spontaneous rhythmic discharges,
of a complex neural network that synchronizes and stabilizes this activity.
This complex is considered the true generator of the respiratory rhythm, because it initiates and maintains the ventilatory cycle.
Lower part contains:
- inspiratory neurons which send efferents to the intercostals, the scalenes.
- expiratory neurons which control the abdominal muscles (recruited during active expiration)
inhibit each other
- receives information from the DNO.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers

blocks.text: The bulbar respiratory centers ensure the regular alternation between inspiration and expiration = respiratory automatism

calm breathing: activation of the bulbar inspiratory neurons → sends efferences to the motor neurons (phrenic nerve and external intercostal nerves), leading to contraction of the inspiratory muscles. A simple interruption of this activation causes the stimulation of the motor neurons to stop → expiration then occurs passively.
Forced expiration: bulbar expiratory neurons become active. They stimulate the motor neurons of the expiratory muscles (internal intercostals, abdominal muscles).

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM A- Respiratory centers

blocks.text: Increased ventilatory requirements: the ventral respiratory group (GRV) is recruited as reinforcement by the dorsal respiratory group (GRD), in order to reinforce both inspiration and expiration.
There is a reciprocal inhibition between inspiratory and expiratory neurons, which allows the alternation of their activation and therefore the regularity of the respiratory cycle.
- the GRD especially plays a role in calm inspiration.
- GRV intervenes mainly during forced breathing
Operating hypotheses: several mechanisms are proposed to explain how certain bulbar neurons generate this respiratory automatism (e.g. intrinsic rhythmic activity, synchronization network).

pages.title: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C- RESPIRATORY CENTERS

blocks.text: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C- RESPIRATORY CENTERS
protuberant respiratory centers modulate the activity of bulbar inspiratory neurons
Apneustics Center
- located in the lower part of the bridge
Stimulates the dorsal respiratory group (DRG), which tends to prolong inspiration.
- its exact role remains poorly known, but it would act as a modulator of the depth and duration of inspiration.
- its action is slowed down by the pneumotaxic center and by vagal afferents (Hering-Breuer reflex).

pages.title: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATION A-RESPIRATORY CENTERS

blocks.text: II-RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATION A-RESPIRATORY CENTERS
pneumotaxic center:
-Located in the upper part of the bridge,
-inactivates inspiratory neurons via the GRD limiting the duration of inspiration.
-modulates the activity of the bulbar centers according to information that comes:
. of the CNS (the hypothalamus: emotion, temperature, etc.)
. and peripheral sensory receptors
is dominant on the apneustic center, which favors the cessation of inspiration and allows expiration to occur.
Respiratory automatism is ensured by the bulbar centers whose activity is modulated by the pneumotaxic center.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS
PaO2 and PaCO2 must remain constant in order for tissuees to function properly. The respiratory system reacts in such a way that:
-if PaO2↘ or PaCO2↗ →Hyperventilation;
-if PaO2↗ or PaCO2↘→Hypoventilation;
-if PH↘ (acidosis)→ Hyperventilation (increased elimination of CO₂).
-if PH↗ (alkalosis) → Hypoventilation (CO₂ retention).
Ventilation (ml/min) = Fr x VT (Fr: respiratory rate VT: Tidal volume)
-↗or↘ventilation→↗or↘Fr
-↗or↘ventilation→↗or↘VT In general both parameters are modified.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB1-peripheral chemoreceptors

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB1-peripheral chemoreceptors
- are located at the level of the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries (carotid glomus), and the arch of the aorta (aortic chemoreceptors).
- They are mainly sensitive to variations in PO₂, and to a lesser extent to variations in blood pH and PaCO₂.
- The generated influx passes through:
. the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) for the carotid bodies,
. the vagus nerve (X) for the aortic corpuscles.
- This information is then transmitted to the bulbar center, which modulates its activity accordingly and adjusts the motor command to the respiratory muscles.
Glossopharyngeal
Sensitive: PO2, pH, PCO2
Sensitive Wave: PO2, pH, PCO2, arterial changes in O2

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB2- central chemoreceptors

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB2- central chemoreceptors
– located on the ventral surface of the bulb
– are stimulated by an increase in PaCO₂, which leads to an increase in the concentration of H⁺ ions in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
– Are not sensitive to PO2

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB2- central chemoreceptors

blocks.text: -In the capillaries in contact with the CSF: thePaCO2 increases =
CO2 diffuses easily from the brain capillary to the CSF across the blood-brain barrier.
-In the CSF:
CO2 + H2O H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-
carbonic anhydrase
These H+ ions directly stimulate central chemoreceptors which in turn excite inspiratory neurons.
In total:
PaCO2↗ →↗CO2in the CSF↗→H+in the CSF→stimulation of central chemoreceptors→activation of bulbar inspiratory neurons→ Hyperventilation →↘PaCO2 →PaCO2 normal.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS B3-CONTROL BY PO2

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS B3-CONTROL BY PO2
A decrease in PaO2 (altitude, hypoxia):
-detected only by peripheral chemoreceptors induces an increase in ventilatory flow
- The response is very fast but not very sensitive
drop in PaO2 < 60 mmHg: an increase in ventilation is noted but remains moderate as long as the oxygen content of the inspired gas is sufficient to maintain an arterial PO2 of 60mmHg.
PaO₂ > 60 mmHg, peripheral chemoreceptors are not very sensitive = ventilation changes little.
PaO₂ < 60 mmHg, stimulation becomes brutal and effective = net increase in ventilatory flow

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB4-CONTROL BY PCO2

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB4-CONTROL BY PCO2
Hypercapnia and acidosis (concomitant changes) are detected by peripheral (CRP) and central (CRC) chemoreceptors.
The answer is:
- very sensitive, and rapid for CRP (PaO₂ ↓, PaCO₂ ↑, pH ↓=in a few seconds= detect acute variations = first alert line)
- slower but powerful for CRC (especially sensitive to PaCO₂ via the pH of the CSF = tens of seconds = ensure sustained and lasting ventilation regulation)
Small increases in arterial PCO2 induce the reflex mechanism of ventilation much more intensely than during the equivalent decrease in PO2.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS CONTROL BY PCO2 and PO2 (curves)

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORS CONTROL BY PCO2 and PO2 (curves)
curve A: the curve is hyperbolic = ventilation stable as long as PaO₂ > 60 mmHg (critical threshold ≈ 60 mmHg)
- PaO2 < 60 mmHg (state of hypoxemia) = strong exponential increase in ventilation
- the central role of peripheral chemoreceptors
(carotid & aortic bodies) which are very sensitive to the drop in oxygen.
In short (Hypoxia): PaO2​ is an emergency regulator of ventilation. Ventilation only increases significantly when oxygen falls to critical levels.
Curve B: quasi-linear.
-ventilation very reactive to variations in PaCO₂= PaCO₂ > 40 mmHg = strong increase;
PaCO₂ < 40 mmHg → decrease.
- central chemoreceptors sensitive to pH (H⁺ of CSF).
Rest: PaCO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg, ventilation ≈ 6–8 L/min.
PaCO₂ is the main regulator of ventilation at rest.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB5-INFLUENCE OF CO₂-INDEPENDENT H⁺

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB5-INFLUENCE OF CO₂-INDEPENDENT H⁺
Metabolic acidosis (e.g. diabetes with ketones, renal failure, lactic acidosis)
-↑ ​​[H⁺] stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors
- Compensatory hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis: ample and rapid breathing) helps eliminate more CO₂ and partially correct the acidosis
Even without variation in PaCO₂, metabolic changes in H⁺ strongly modify respiration.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB6-Potentiating effect

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM B-CHEMORECEPTORSB6-Potentiating effect
Chemoreceptors respond to both hypoxia (decrease in PaO₂) and hypercapnia (increase in PaCO₂).
When they are stimulated together, there is a potentiating effect: hypoxia increases ventilatory sensitivity to CO₂ and vice versa = the two signals add up and reinforce each other.
Low PaO₂ + high PaCO₂ results in a much stronger ventilatory response than the sum of the separate effects.
It is a safety mechanism allowing rapid hyperventilation to be triggered when the body is in danger (lack of O₂ and excess CO₂).

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORSSC1- Héring-Breuer reflex

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORSSC1- Héring-Breuer reflex
It is a protective reflex that prevents excessive inflation of the lungs during very deep inspirations (e.g. during exercise).
Significant pulmonary inflation Pulmonary stretch receptors in the smooth muscle layer of the airways vagal afferents towards the centers inhibition of inspiratory neurons.
Hering-Breuer: lungs too inflated → vagus nerve → stop inspiration.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORS C2-Spinal reflexes (myotatic reflex)

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORS C2-Spinal reflexes (myotatic reflex)

During expiration linked to the relaxation of the inspiratory muscles (especially the external intercostal muscles), they lengthen, causing their activation by myotatic reflex = contributes to maintaining a certain rhythm and respiratory tone = a mechanism for fine regulation of the ventilatory cycle.
this reflex has a medullary integration center, but it is under the control of the respiratory bulb centers.
Myotatic: lengthening of inspiratory muscles → spinal cord → automatic reactivation.
Hering-Breuer and myotatic reflexes = automatic regulation of rhythm.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORSSC3-Protective respiratory reflexes

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM C-PULMONARY MECHANORECEPTORSSC3-Protective respiratory reflexes
- receptors of the large bronchi, trachea, larynx: stimulated by inhaled particles and irritating gases = cough reflex as well as constriction of the larynx and bronchi.
- receptors in the smaller bronchi and in the bronchioles: stimulated by irritating particles = bronchoconstriction.
- J receptors present in the capillary wall or in the interstitium, normally quiescent; stimulated by interstitial edema or venous hyperpressure leading to respiratory difficulty.
- nasal receptors: stimulated by dust, pollen or other irritants → sneeze reflex, which suddenly expels air through the nose and mouth to protect the upper respiratory tract.
airway protection reflexes.

pages.title: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM EXTRA-PULMONARY RESPIRATORY REGULATION

blocks.text: II- RESPIRATORY CENTERS AND AUTOMATISM EXTRA-PULMONARY RESPIRATORY REGULATION
-Baroreceptors (carotid sinus, aortic arch) send signals to the medulla oblongata.
.↓ Blood pressure → stimulation of breathing. (to improve venous return and oxygenation).
.↑ Blood pressure → breathing brake
- Acute pain → stimulates the respiratory centers = reflex hyperventilation.
-Fever → increases ventilation due to:
.increased metabolism (higher production of CO₂),
.systemic inflammation acting on the respiratory centers.

-Behavioral regulation allows voluntary control of breathing by the cortex. this voluntary regulation is limited and cannot oppose reflex mechanisms indefinitely. It adapts ventilation to behaviors (speech, singing, coughing, apnea) and emotions.

Speech, swallowing, yawning, sneezing…. indirectly stimulate the respiratory centers It has a protective (prevention of aspiration, cough) and anticipatory (ventilation to behavioral needs) role, completing automatic regulation.

pages.title: III- III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS A-DURING EXERCISE

blocks.text: III- III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS A-DURING EXERCISE
During muscular exercise, ventilation increases immediately, often even before changes in PO₂, PCO₂ or pH are observed in the blood = control does not depend solely on chemoreceptors.
Central control
The cerebral motor center simultaneously activates:
- Skeletal muscle motor neurons
- Bulbar respiratory centers
Anticipated increase in ventilation from the start of the effort

pages.title: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS A-DURING EXERCISE

blocks.text: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS A-DURING EXERCISE
Peripheral afferents
Muscle and joint receptors (mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors) transmit signals to the respiratory centers and adjust ventilation proportional to the intensity of the effort.
Role of chemoreceptors
-Moderate exercise: PO₂, PCO₂ and pH remain stable fine adjustment.
-Intense exercise: lactic acid production metabolic acidosis additional ventilatory stimulation.

pages.title: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS B-ACCLIMATION TO HIGH ALTITUDE

blocks.text: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS B-ACCLIMATION TO HIGH ALTITUDE

At altitude, atmospheric pressure reduces the PO₂ of the inspired air and reduces arterial hypoxia = the body brings several adaptation mechanisms into play: ventilatory, renal, hematological and tissuee.
- Immediate ventilatory response
Hypoxia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic glomus) reflex hyperventilation decrease in PCO₂ respiratory alkalosis partial inhibition of ventilation (temporary)
- Renal compensation: in a few days, the kidney:- excretes more bicarbonates (HCO₃⁻).- restores blood pH.- allows the maintenance of lasting hyperventilation.

pages.title: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS B-ACCLIMATION TO HIGH ALTITUDE

blocks.text: Hematological adaptations
-Hypoxia stimulates the secretion of erythropoietin: erythropoiesis hematocrit and hemoglobin
- 2,3-DPG in red blood cells facilitates the release of O₂ to tissuees.
Cardiovascular and tissuee adaptations
-initial phase: cardiac output to compensate for the drop in O₂.
-chronic phase: normalization of cardiac output.
-tissuees: capillary density and mitochondrial adaptations better use of O₂.

pages.title: III- CONTROL OF VENTILATION SPECIAL PHYSIOLOGICAL CONDITIONS B-ACCLIMATION TO HIGH ALTITUDE

blocks.text: Limits of acclimatization
- Arterial O₂ saturation remains lower than at sea level.
- ascent too rapid → acute mountain sickness, sometimes pulmonary or cerebral edema.
In short, acclimatization is based on:
- rapid ventilatory stimulation (peripheral chemoreceptors),
- renal compensation to correct alkalosis,
- and hematological and tissuee adaptations to improve the transport and use of oxygen.
= maintenance of sufficient tissuee oxygenation despite the drop in ambient PO₂.

pages.title: SUMMARY

blocks.text: SUMMARY
Respiratory centers: Located in the medulla and pons, these nerve centers generate basic respiratory rhythms and integrate information from receptors.
Receptors:

-Central chemoreceptors: Located in the medulla oblongata, they are sensitive to variations in the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid, which reflect variations in the partial pressure of CO2 in the arterial blood.
-Peripheral chemoreceptors: Located in the carotids and the aorta, they are sensitive to variations in the partial pressure of O2 and CO2 in arterial blood.
-Mechanoreceptors: Located in the lungs and airways, they inform the respiratory centers about the state of distension of the lungs.
Effectors: The respiratory muscles (diaphragm, intercostal muscles) are innervated by the phrenic and intercostal nerves, under the control of the respiratory centers.

pages.title: Summary

blocks.text: Summary
Regulatory Mechanisms = reflex and voluntary mechanisms.
Reflex regulation: Receptors send information to the respiratory centers which, in return, adjust ventilation = rapid and automatic regulation.
Voluntary regulation: Breathing can be voluntarily modified, for example: when speaking, apnea. this voluntary regulation is limited.
